lead.headline: Ridgewood girl of nine wins the children's recording contest
lead.deck: Minute of her grandmother singing in Hungarian chosen from 7,112 entries; record sealed into the Phonautograph Society's vault for 1978; Long Island City boy's night record retained for further hearing
lead.body: Miss Ilona Farkas, nine, of Ridgewood, won the children's recording contest of the Parks Department at Borough Hall at 3:20 p.m. yesterday with one minute of her grandmother, Mrs. Erzsebet Farkas, 71, singing a Hungarian cradle song, Commissioner Ambrose Tuttle states. The judges heard 7,112 entries in eleven days. Miss Farkas received a fifteen-dollar home recorder. The record was sealed into the Society's vault for 1978 at 4 p.m. The record of a Long Island City boy's street at night is retained 'for further hearing.'

columns.headline: Graf Zeppelin passes north of Moscow; course over Vologda for the Urals
columns.body: The Graf Zeppelin passed north of Moscow at about 11 a.m. yesterday, New York time, without circling the city, and set her course over Vologda for the Urals, the Berlin wire states. The Soviet station at Moscow recorded her engines and played them on its evening service.

columns.headline: Mr. Ewald writes to the company's box a second time, asking what is held
columns.body: Mr. Nathan Ewald posted a second letter to the post box of Signal Ground Rents Inc. at Long Island City at 9:15 a.m. yesterday, asking 'what is held, by whom, and until when.' The box was otherwise empty at noon. The court clerk holds 1,236 dollars.

columns.headline: Stocks rise on 4,100,000 shares; ticker's tone entered as 'bright'
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange rose yesterday on a volume of 4,100,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 358.1, a gain of 3.4. The ticker ran 12 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'bright.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Mild. High 81. Friday. Twenty Fridays. Grandma's in the vault.

lead.headline: Grandma's lullaby takes the prize, and the vault puts 1978 on hold
lead.deck: Seven thousand one hundred and twelve children, one winner: a Ridgewood girl of nine and a cradle song sung by a lady of seventy-one who did not know she was entered
lead.body: Out of seven thousand one hundred and twelve minutes of dogs, fires, goats and the Sidewalks of New York, the judges picked Ilona Farkas of Ridgewood, nine, who held the recorder up to her grandmother while the old lady sang a cradle song in Hungarian. Mrs. Farkas did not know she was being recorded. She knows now. The record went into the Society's vault for 1978. Ilona got the home recorder. The judges have gone home to lie down in a quiet room.

columns.headline: Pun Derby, week eleven: a Woodhaven baker gets a rise out of the judges
columns.body: Week eleven goes to Mrs. Hedda Lutz, baker, of Woodhaven: 'My bread is like the Hum. It comes up at night, and nobody at the light company will admit to it.' Five dollars and a year's Speaker. Mr. Kehoe's horse sent nothing this week. The judges are worried.

columns.headline: Party Line's twentieth Friday, and the parcel window rings hollow
columns.body: Twenty Fridays. Party Line at the window at four, tail round her feet. At five, back under the board. No tin from Corona. Sergeant Moran was seen at the linemen's lodge on Wednesday, bowling. He bowled badly. He says that is what a coincidence looks like.

columns.headline: Ewald writes the company again, and asks it to expand on 'Held'
columns.body: Mr. Ewald has posted the company a second letter, asking what is held, by whom and until when. Three questions, to a company that has spent two months on one word. The Arcade pool will not take bets on this one. The cigar stand says it has feelings.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The Graf skips Moscow, and Moscow plays her engines on the evening radio anyway. Everybody hears; nobody waves.

lead.headline: Week's count: 2,390 night calls on the tone in Queens; Brooklyn door at 1,301
lead.deck: Rise of 176 on the week, the fourth weekly rise; operators' sheets enter 'steady' and 'close'; Dr. Rastin's Corona readings unchanged at two fifths above June; light company does not comment
lead.body: The Queens Exchange logged 2,390 calls between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. in the seven nights to Friday reporting a tone, against 2,214, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states, the fourth weekly rise. The operators' sheets describe the tone as 'steady' and 'close.' Dr. Emil Rastin states that his Corona readings for the week are unchanged, at about two fifths above June between midnight and 4 a.m. The Brooklyn Exchange's door shows 1,301. Queens Light & Power states that it does not comment.

columns.headline: No parcel for Position 43 on a twentieth Friday
columns.body: No parcel addressed to 'Party Line, Queens Exchange, Position 43' was received yesterday, the twentieth Friday without one, the supervisor states. The animal attended the parcel window from 4 p.m. to 5 p.m. The warrant for Mr. Joseph Marchetti, lineman, remains outstanding.

columns.headline: Graf Zeppelin over Siberia; no message received in America for 19 hours
columns.body: No message from the Graf Zeppelin had been received by the Navy or the Radio Corporation for 19 hours at midnight, the ship being over Siberia beyond the reach of any American station, the Navy states. The Berlin wire last placed her near Tobolsk. Tokyo expects her on Monday.

columns.headline: Mr. Crane borrows six clerks to inspect his 62 inspectors a second time
columns.body: Mr. Hollis Crane has asked the Borough President to lend six clerks to inspect the residences of his 62 licence inspectors a second time, the first inspection having been made by the inspectors of one another, his office states. The 14 found unlicensed have 26 days remaining to apply.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states, at any of its four places.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 83. Saturday. Twenty-three hundred calls. The Hum keeps its number.

lead.headline: Crane's inspectors get a second hearing, from six borrowed clerks
lead.deck: Sixty-two licence men inspected each other last week and fourteen came up short; now the Borough President's clerks go round again, and nobody in the office will say who checks the clerks
lead.body: Last week Mr. Crane's sixty-two licence inspectors went round each other's houses in pairs, and fourteen were found with listening systems nobody had licensed. This week Mr. Crane has asked the Borough President for six clerks to go round again, since a man inspected by a colleague he has just inspected may have been, as the office puts it, 'generous.' The clerks start Monday. The Ridgewood landlord who began all this has offered his services. Mr. Crane says he will keep the offer on file.

columns.headline: Twenty-three hundred calls, and the operators write the Hum down as 'close'
columns.body: Two thousand three hundred and ninety calls this week about the night tone, up again, the fourth week running. The operators' sheets used to say 'nearer.' Now they say 'close.' Dr. Rastin's meter says the same as last week. The light company says nothing, which is also the same.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Siberia, says the office boy, and he has a pin for it
columns.body: Five weeks of Mr. Pike's four places, and sixteen-ten silent at all of them. The Graf is over Siberia, where nobody can hear her either. The office boy has put a pin in Tobolsk. The editor has taken it out. It is back.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: a Halloran girl says I do, and the parish plays it back
columns.body: Darlings, the elder Halloran girl married Mr. Desmond Clery this afternoon at St. Joan of Arc, Jackson Heights, and the parish lent its recorder. The bride had the vows played at the breakfast. The groom asked for once. They were played twice. Mrs. Van Ness wore the mooring-mast hat again.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Six o'clock: Ruthie Danko of Sunnyside reports the terrier on her step three days early, in a new red collar. Nobody's.

editorial.headline: Five hundred home runs and one woman out at home
editorial.body: Babe Ruth hit his five hundredth home run on Sunday and this paper, like every paper, salutes him. Babe Ruth is a man. When he strikes out the crowd forgives him, because a man is permitted to swing and miss. A woman who swings, in our view, should not miss either, and Lilith has not missed once this year, which is why we distrust her. This week she struck out Magistrate Teague for the second time, persuading him at a supper dance to release the last eight girls he sent to Bedford for waywardness. They came home on Friday. Teague says he does not remember signing. He remembers the soup.

lead.headline: Elevated guard buried at Calvary; trains on the Flushing line stand one minute
lead.deck: Mr. Thomas Rourke, 44, dead of blood poisoning eleven days after cutting his hand on a gate latch at Junction Boulevard; about 600 attend; the minute recorded by the line's own system
lead.body: Mr. Thomas Rourke, 44, a guard on the Flushing elevated for nineteen years, was buried at Calvary Cemetery yesterday after a Requiem Mass at Our Lady of Sorrows, Corona. He died on Wednesday of blood poisoning, eleven days after cutting his hand on a gate latch at Junction Boulevard. About 600 attended. At 10 a.m. every train on the line stood for one minute, the Interborough states, and the line's system recorded the minute. He leaves a widow and four children.

columns.headline: Miss Halloran married to Mr. Clery at St. Joan of Arc; vows recorded
columns.body: Miss Agnes Halloran, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Patrick Halloran of Jackson Heights, was married to Mr. Desmond Clery, a junction-man of the Queens Exchange, at St. Joan of Arc at 4 p.m. yesterday. The vows were recorded by the parish and played at the breakfast, twice, at the bride's request.

columns.headline: Stocks close the week at 361.5 at a short session; tone 'climbing'
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange closed the week at yesterday's short session on a volume of 2,380,000 shares, the industrial average standing at 361.5, a gain on the week of 12.4. The ticker was 6 minutes late at noon. Its tone was entered as 'climbing.'

columns.headline: Graf Zeppelin reported over Yakutsk; Kasumigaura readies its shed
columns.body: The Graf Zeppelin was over Yakutsk at about 2 p.m. yesterday, New York time, the Berlin wire states, by way of the Japanese naval station at Ominato, which heard her first. The Imperial Navy's shed at Kasumigaura, brought from Germany after the war, is ready. About 300 sailors are on the field.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Warm. High 85. Sunday. Church, dinner, bed. The usual hum.

lead.headline: The terrier crashes the Halloran wedding and gets his bark on the record
lead.deck: Red collar, brown ear, no invitation; the parish recorder takes down the vows, the organ and one dog at the word 'obey'; three owners now want a copy of somebody else's wedding
lead.body: The elder Halloran girl married Mr. Desmond Clery at St. Joan of Arc yesterday, and at the word 'obey' a wire-haired terrier in a new red collar barked once from the back pew. The parish recorder took it down. The usher put him out. Within the hour Mrs. Fitch, Dr. Voight and Mrs. Ahl had each asked the parish for a copy of the record, to identify the bark. The parish says the record belongs to the bride. The bride says the dog may keep his part.

columns.headline: The El stands still a minute, and the line holds for a guard
columns.body: At ten yesterday morning every train on the Flushing line stopped for one minute for Tom Rourke, guard, nineteen years on the platforms, dead of a cut hand. The line's own system recorded the minute. Riders say it was the quietest the El has ever been. His widow has asked for the record.

columns.headline: The Graf drops off the line over Siberia, and the Japanese pick up
columns.body: Nineteen hours without a word, then the Japanese Navy's station at Ominato heard her over Yakutsk and passed it on. Tokyo is ready with a shed it got from Germany after the war, which means the Graf is going to sleep in her cousin's bed.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Why is it so quiet on a Sunday?'
columns.body: Madam, it is not quiet; it is Sunday. The trolleys run less, the trucks stop, the mills shut, and you notice what is left: your clock, your husband and the tone. The operator notices too. She says Sunday night is when she can hear the board breathe.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Eleven o'clock: Corona reports the tone 'about as usual.' The Speaker goes to bed.

lead.headline: Yankees divide a double-header with St. Louis; the Athletics lead by fourteen
lead.deck: Mr. Ruth's thirty-second home run in the second game; about 52,000 at the Stadium; the Athletics win again at Shibe Park; Brooklyn loses, the Giants win
lead.body: The Yankees divided a double-header with the St. Louis Browns at the Stadium yesterday before about 52,000, losing the first game by 4 to 2 and winning the second by 7 to 3, Mr. Babe Ruth hitting his thirty-second home run of the season in the seventh inning. The Athletics won at Shibe Park and lead the American League by fourteen games. Brooklyn lost at Ebbets Field. The Giants won at the Polo Grounds. The Stadium's own record of the double-header runs to five hours.

columns.headline: Graf Zeppelin expected at Kasumigaura this morning, New York time
columns.body: The Graf Zeppelin was over the Sea of Okhotsk at 6 p.m. yesterday, New York time, and is expected at Kasumigaura, near Tokyo, at about 6 a.m. today, the Berlin wire states. This newspaper's window on Jackson Avenue will play the Tokyo wire as received.

columns.headline: Central Trades and Labor Council files its route for the Labor Day parade
columns.body: The Central Trades and Labor Council of Queens has filed with the Police Department its route for the Labor Day parade on September 2, from Jamaica Avenue at 168th Street to King Park, the Council states. About 9,000 are expected to march, among them, for the first time, the Queens Exchange operators.

columns.headline: Mr. Crane's six borrowed clerks begin the second inspection today
columns.body: The six clerks lent by the Borough President to Mr. Hollis Crane's office will begin today to inspect the residences of the office's 62 licence inspectors, his office states. Inspectors are asked to be at home between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., and to say nothing.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Queens Exchange reports calls from 12:04 a.m. stating that the tone has stopped. The Exchange is logging them.

speaker.ear: Warm. High 84. Monday. Listen. No, really. Listen.

lead.headline: The Hum hangs up on Queens, and the whole borough is left on hold
lead.deck: Not a note since four minutes past midnight; Dr. Rastin's meter on the Corona roof reads nothing at all; the operators take the busiest day in the Exchange's history from people ringing to report nothing
lead.body: At four minutes past midnight the tone stopped. Not quieter: stopped. Dr. Rastin's meter on the Corona roof fell to nothing and has stayed there. By breakfast the Queens Exchange had taken more calls than on Armistice night, every one of them saying the same thing, which is that they could not hear anything. Corona did not sleep. Woodside sat on its stoops. A Maspeth baby who hums along has stopped humming. The light company says its load today is 'as on any Monday.' Nobody believes Monday.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Where has the Hum gone?'
columns.body: Madam, the operator does not know. She has been asked four thousand times since midnight and has written down, four thousand times, 'tone absent.' She would add that her board has never sounded so loud. Every relay in the Exchange can be heard. So can her own heart. She did not care for it.

columns.headline: The Graf rings Tokyo's doorbell, and a quarter of a million answer
columns.body: The Graf Zeppelin came down at Kasumigaura this morning at four minutes to six our time, a hundred and one hours from Friedrichshafen. The Tokyo wire played in the Record's window at seven, to a crowd that had come to hear the Japanese cheer and stayed because, for once, there was nothing else to hear.

columns.headline: The Circle goes out to record Flushing with nothing left to filter out
columns.body: Mr. Moss of the Flushing Circle was on the Meadow at noon with the Circle's recorder, taking down the dumps 'as they are today.' He did not need his filter. Mrs. Grieve came along and said nothing for an hour. Then she said it sounded like a waiting room.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Nine o'clock tonight. Still nothing. Corona's lights are all on. A man on Junction Boulevard is playing a record of the Hum, loud, to get to sleep.

columns.headline: Astoria's ferry gets a new whistle, and Astoria would like the old one back
columns.body: The Astoria ferry has been fitted with a new steam whistle at the owners' expense, and it has been heard as far off as Whitestone by persons who had not asked. Forty-four letters have reached this desk. All of them are shorter than the whistle.

columns.headline: The Pun Derby: this week's winner has nothing to say, and says it well
columns.body: This week's five dollars goes to a Jamaica lady who says that the quiet in Queens is deafening, that she can't hear herself think, and that her husband has noticed the improvement. The night desk has sent him the five dollars instead.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: a heat-struck August, and nobody's business but ours
columns.body: Darlings, Rockaway is full of people who told their families they were in Rockaway. Crepe de chine has given up. A Kew Gardens gentleman is taking the waters with a lady who is not, the Listening Lady hears, the waters. More on Thursday.

columns.headline: Twenty lady fliers leave for Cleveland; our desk attends to powder
columns.body: Twenty women fliers left Santa Monica yesterday for Cleveland in the transcontinental air derby, which Mr. Will Rogers has named the Powder Puff Derby. The route runs two thousand eight hundred miles. Our aviation editor is prepared to report on powder as soon as a correspondent finds any.

back.foot: The Speaker. Read it before somebody reads it to you.

lead.headline: Tone absent in Queens and Brooklyn for 24 hours; returns at 12:02 a.m.
lead.deck: Dr. Rastin's meter reads no tone at 41 cycles from 12:04 a.m. Monday; Queens Exchange logs 4,870 calls reporting its absence; light company states its load was 'as on any Monday'
lead.body: The tone at 41 cycles was absent in Queens and Brooklyn from 12:04 a.m. yesterday until 12:02 a.m. today, Dr. Emil Rastin states from his readings in Corona, and returned at its former strength. The Queens Exchange logged 4,870 calls reporting its absence, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states, the most in one day in the Exchange's history. Jamaica Hospital treated 31 persons for want of sleep. Queens Light & Power states that its load yesterday was 'as on any Monday' and that it has nothing further to state.

columns.headline: Graf Zeppelin moored at Kasumigaura 101 hours from Friedrichshafen
columns.body: The Graf Zeppelin was walked into the naval shed at Kasumigaura at 5:56 a.m. yesterday, New York time, about 101 hours from Friedrichshafen, the Berlin wire states. About 250,000 persons were on the field. Dr. Hugo Eckener stated that Siberia had been 'quiet.' She leaves for Los Angeles on Friday, New York time.

columns.headline: Phonautograph Circle records Flushing Meadow during the tone's absence
columns.body: Mr. Irving Moss, president of the Phonautograph Circle of Flushing, recorded the Flushing Meadow dumps from noon to 12:20 p.m. yesterday without the filter, the tone being absent, he states. The Circle will hear the record at the library tomorrow night. Mrs. Ottoline Grieve attended the recording.

columns.headline: Stocks rise to 365.2 on 4,450,000 shares; tone book enters 'running'
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange rose yesterday on a volume of 4,450,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 365.2, a gain of 3.7 and the highest of the year. The ticker ran 19 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'running.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states. The Division states that it heard nothing else either.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 82. Tuesday. It's back. Go to sleep.

lead.headline: The Hum comes home at two past midnight and won't say where it's been
lead.deck: Twenty-four hours of dead air, forty-eight hundred calls, thirty-one in the hospital for want of sleep, and then, at two minutes past twelve, the old forty-one cycles as if nothing had happened
lead.body: At two minutes past midnight the tone came back. Same pitch, same strength, Dr. Rastin says, as if it had stepped out for a paper. In Corona a cheer went up from the stoops, and then everybody went to bed and slept like stones. By morning Queens had overslept by an hour; milk was late in Woodhaven and the El ran half empty until nine. The light company says Monday's load was as on any Monday. Nobody has explained Monday. Nobody, we notice, has tried.

columns.headline: Forty-eight hundred calls to report nothing, and the Exchange rings up a record
columns.body: Four thousand eight hundred and seventy people rang the Queens operators on Monday to tell them the tone had gone. The operators knew. Superintendent Arne says it is the busiest day the Exchange has ever had. The second busiest was the Armistice. He says he would rather have the Armistice.

columns.headline: The dog war: the terrier sings all through the quiet, and signs off at midnight
columns.body: The terrier was on Ruthie Danko's Sunnyside step all of Monday, howling from breakfast to bedtime, the neighbours say, 'to fill the space.' At two past midnight he stopped and went to sleep on the mat. Ruthie recorded him. Three owners have asked for copies.

columns.headline: The Graf parks in Tokyo, and a quarter of a million turn up the volume
columns.body: A quarter of a million Japanese were on the field at Kasumigaura when the Graf was walked into her borrowed shed. Dr. Eckener said Siberia had been quiet. Queens would like a word with him about quiet. She leaves for Los Angeles on Friday.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Dr. Rastin, asked at six tonight what happened on Monday, said 'It stopped,' and went back up to the roof.

lead.headline: Board of Aldermen asks Queens Light & Power to account for Monday's tone
lead.deck: Resolution of Alderman Feeney carried by 41 votes to 9; company to reply in writing within ten days; company states that it 'did nothing on Monday' and will reply
lead.body: The Board of Aldermen yesterday carried by 41 votes to 9 a resolution of Alderman John Feeney of Queens asking Queens Light & Power to state in writing within ten days what occurred on its system between 12:04 a.m. Monday and 12:02 a.m. Tuesday. Mr. Feeney entered the Queens Exchange's log of 4,870 calls. The company stated last night that it 'did nothing on Monday' and would reply. Mr. Feeney's application for the records of the 23 disputed primary districts will be heard on October 9.

columns.headline: Mr. Gorman asks for the calendar of September 23; 'thirty-four days'
columns.body: Mr. Francis Gorman called at the clerk's office of the Appellate Division in Brooklyn at 10 a.m. yesterday and asked for the calendar for September 23, the clerk states. None has been printed. Mr. Gorman stated that it was 'thirty-four days' and left.

columns.headline: Senate vault's record of March 27 unclaimed in its twenty-second week
columns.body: Mr. Lyman Pratt, Clerk of the Senate, states that the committee room's record of March 27 containing the word 'resent' remains unclaimed in the vault at Albany in its twenty-second week. Senator Rufus Keel has written to ask whether the vault 'heard Monday.' Mr. Pratt has replied that the vault is in Albany.

columns.headline: Phonautograph Circle meets tonight to hear Monday's record of the Meadow
columns.body: The Phonautograph Circle of Flushing meets at 8 p.m. tonight at the Flushing Free Library to hear Mr. Irving Moss's record of the Flushing Meadow dumps, made on Monday during the tone's absence. Mrs. Ottoline Grieve has withdrawn her notice of a motion, Mr. Moss states.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

columns.headline: Miss Marvel Crosson found dead in Arizona; a competitor in the women's air derby
columns.body: Miss Marvel Crosson, a competitor in the women's air derby from Santa Monica to Cleveland, was found dead yesterday near her machine in a ravine by the Gila River near Wellton, Arizona, the wire states. She had not arrived at Phoenix on Monday. The derby continues.

columns.headline: Board of Water Supply asks householders to spare the hydrants this week
columns.body: The Board of Water Supply asks householders in Corona and Elmhurst to refrain from opening hydrants this week, the Board states, as pressure has been low on upper floors. Offenders are liable to a fine. Sprinklers are permitted before 8 a.m.

columns.headline: Peaches plentiful at Wallabout Market; ice unchanged at the wagon
columns.body: Georgia and Jersey peaches were plentiful at the Wallabout Market yesterday, and sold lower by the basket, dealers state. Sweet corn from Nassau was in good supply. Ice was unchanged at the wagon. Butter was firm, and eggs were steady.

columns.headline: Fair weather to hold through Friday, the Weather Bureau states
columns.body: The Weather Bureau forecasts fair skies through Friday, with a high near 80 and a low of 64 today. Light winds from the northwest are expected. Bathing conditions at Rockaway were reported as good yesterday by the Parks Department.

back.foot: The Borough Record, Long Island City. Corrections are printed as received.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 80. Wednesday. The aldermen want a word. The company has one.

lead.headline: Aldermen ring the light company about Monday, and get the usual dial tone
lead.deck: Forty-one to nine, Alderman Feeney wants it in writing within ten days; the company says it did nothing on Monday, which is what it says it does every day
lead.body: Alderman Feeney stood up in the Board yesterday with the Exchange's log of forty-eight hundred calls under his arm and asked the light company, in writing, what happened to the tone on Monday. The Board voted forty-one to nine to ask with him. The company answered before the ink was dry: it did nothing on Monday. It will say so again, in writing, within ten days. The nine who voted no were all from Manhattan, which has never had a tone to lose.

columns.headline: Gorman says thirty-four days, and the clerk's line stays engaged
columns.body: Tuesday at ten, the Appellate Division clerk's window in Brooklyn: Mr. Gorman, for the calendar of the twenty-third of September. Not printed. 'Thirty-four days,' says Mr. Gorman, and goes. We have counted again. He is right again. He is the most punctual man in Brooklyn.

columns.headline: Week twenty-two: Keel asks whether 'resent' heard the quiet
columns.body: Twenty-two weeks in the vault at Albany. This week Senator Keel wrote to ask whether the vault heard Monday. Mr. Pratt wrote back that the vault is in Albany. The Speaker has checked a map. Mr. Pratt is right. The Senator has not yet written back.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Silent on the quiet day, and Pike won't read into it
columns.body: On Monday, with the whole borough listening harder than it ever has, Mr. Pike's four places heard nothing on sixteen-ten either. The office boy wanted to put a pin in Monday. The editor says you cannot pin a day. The office boy has pinned the calendar.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Flushing Library, nine o'clock: the Circle hears Monday's record of the Meadow. Mrs. Grieve leaves the room in the second minute.

lead.headline: Phonautograph Circle votes 17 to 0 not to keep Monday's record of the Meadow
lead.deck: Record of the dumps made during the tone's absence heard at the library; Mrs. Grieve leaves in the second minute; the record to be returned to Mr. Moss unfiled; no reason entered
lead.body: The Phonautograph Circle of Flushing heard Mr. Irving Moss's record of the Flushing Meadow dumps, made on Monday during the tone's absence, at the Flushing Free Library last night, Mr. Moss states. Mrs. Ottoline Grieve left the room in the second minute. The Circle then voted by 17 votes to none that the record not be kept, and that it be returned to Mr. Moss unfiled. No reason was entered. Mr. Moss states that the Circle's vote of August 7, nine to eight, stands.

columns.headline: Stocks rise to 368.9 on 4,620,000 shares; tone book enters 'running'
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange rose yesterday on a volume of 4,620,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 368.9, a gain of 2.2 and the highest in its history. The ticker ran 21 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'running' again.

columns.headline: Signal Exchange's advertisement for the Ditmars Avenue owner answered from Ohio
columns.body: The Queens Signal Exchange's advertisement for the owner of the house on Ditmars Avenue has been answered by a Cleveland attorney, Mr. Royal Haskin, acting for an estate he does not name, the Exchange states. Mr. Hollis Crane states that the seal remains until the owner attends in person.

columns.headline: Graf Zeppelin to leave Kasumigaura for Los Angeles early tomorrow
columns.body: The Graf Zeppelin will leave Kasumigaura for Los Angeles at about 1 a.m. tomorrow, New York time, a flight of about 5,500 miles across the Pacific, the Berlin wire states. No ship of the air has crossed the Pacific without a stop. The Navy's stations on the Pacific coast will sit from Saturday.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Warmer. High 84. Thursday. The Circle has heard enough of nothing.

lead.headline: Wall Street hits its highest pitch, and the ticker can't keep up with the tune
lead.deck: Three hundred and sixty-nine on the industrials, twenty-one minutes of ticker behind the floor, and every barber in Queens with a tip he heard from a man who heard it
lead.body: Stocks climbed again yesterday, the industrials at three hundred and sixty-nine, the highest ever, and the ticker ran twenty-one minutes behind the floor, like a man reading the news aloud to people who have already heard it. The tone book says 'running.' In Jamaica a dentist has bought Radio on margin. In Flushing an undertaker has bought Steel. A Kew Gardens widow has bought both and a fur. The Speaker's financial editor has bought lunch, which he describes as his position.

columns.headline: The Circle votes seventeen to nothing to switch off Monday's record
columns.body: Mr. Moss played the Circle his Monday record of the Flushing dumps, the one with no tone to take out. Mrs. Grieve left in the second minute. Then all seventeen voted not to keep it. Nobody gave a reason. Mr. Abbot, still uninvited, says he could have told them.

columns.headline: A Cleveland lawyer answers for the Ditmars house, and won't give out the number
columns.body: The Exchange advertised for the owner of the house on Ditmars Avenue, where the sealed room heard the fire first, and got an answer from Cleveland: a Mr. Haskin, for an estate he will not name. Mr. Crane says the owner must come in person. Cleveland says it will be in touch.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Who is Box 61?'
columns.body: Madam, the operator does not know and the Record will not say. Somebody mislaid some plates at an Arcade counter and the reward has gone to fifty dollars. A man who leaves his plates with a stranger and then advertises for them has either a very good picture or a very bad one.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Kasumigaura, this afternoon their time: the Graf takes on gas and two Japanese naval officers. The office boy asks if they need a third.

lead.headline: Graf Zeppelin leaves Kasumigaura for Los Angeles across the Pacific
lead.deck: Ship away at 1:13 a.m. today, New York time, with 20 passengers and two officers of the Imperial Navy; about 5,500 miles to the coast; the Navy's stations at San Diego and San Francisco to sit from Saturday
lead.body: The Graf Zeppelin left Kasumigaura for Los Angeles at 1:13 a.m. today, New York time, the Berlin wire states, with 20 passengers, among them two officers of the Imperial Japanese Navy, and Dr. Hugo Eckener in command. The flight of about 5,500 miles would be the first crossing of the Pacific by air without a stop. The Navy's stations at San Diego and San Francisco will sit from Saturday. Her first message reached this newspaper's office at 2:40 a.m. and read 'Coast behind.'

columns.headline: Third postcard from Dr. Strand shows the chapel from nearer; no message
columns.body: Union Seminary states that it received a third postcard from Dr. Matthias Strand yesterday, posted at Bangor on August 12. It shows the same chapel as the first two, taken from nearer, the door being visible. The reverse bears the address and nothing else. The seminary chapel reopens on September 16.

columns.headline: Arcade tenants to meet tonight on the September rent
columns.body: The tenants of the Vantry Arcade will meet at the luncheonette at 8 p.m. tonight to decide whether to deposit the September rent of 412 dollars with the Municipal Court clerk, Mr. Nathan Ewald states. Mr. Ewald's letter of August 15 to the company's box has not been answered.

columns.headline: Second inspection finds three more licence inspectors unlicensed
columns.body: The six clerks lent by the Borough President have found unlicensed systems in the residences of three more of Mr. Hollis Crane's 62 licence inspectors, his office states, the three having been passed by their colleagues earlier in the month. The unlicensed now number 17. They continue to inspect.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 85. Friday. Twenty-one Fridays. The Graf's gone to sea.

lead.headline: The Graf places the long-distance call: Tokyo to Los Angeles, no operator
lead.deck: Nobody has flown the Pacific in one go; at thirteen past one this morning Dr. Eckener cast off to try, with twenty passengers, two Japanese officers and fifty-five hundred miles of water ahead
lead.body: Nobody has ever flown the Pacific in one go. At thirteen minutes past one this morning the Graf Zeppelin cast off at Kasumigaura to try, with twenty passengers, two Japanese naval officers and fifty-five hundred miles of water between her and California. Her first wire, 'Coast behind,' reached the Record's office at twenty to three. After that the Pacific has her. The Navy sits at San Diego from tomorrow. Our office boy sits at Jackson Avenue from tonight, with the blanket.

columns.headline: Pun Derby, week twelve: a cabbie puts the Hum's day off on the meter
columns.body: Week twelve goes to Mr. Sal Ruggiero, cab driver, of Astoria: 'The Hum took Monday off. First thing in Queens to get a holiday before Labor Day, and the only one that came back on time.' Five dollars and a year's Speaker. The grand final is on Labor Day.

columns.headline: Party Line's twenty-first Friday: still no package on the line
columns.body: Twenty-one Fridays. Party Line at the window at four. Tail. Grille. At five, under the board. No tin from Corona. Sergeant Moran has joined the linemen's bowling team, under the name of Smith. Nobody at the lodge is fooled. Nobody has said so.

columns.headline: Strand's third postcard draws nearer, and the line on the back stays blank
columns.body: The third postcard from Dr. Strand came yesterday: the same Welsh chapel, but nearer, so you can see the door. On the back, the address and nothing else. Our Chester cousin says the next one will be from inside. The seminary says its own chapel reopens on the sixteenth.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Arcade luncheonette, ten o'clock: the tenants vote to pay September into court on the third. Ewald to carry it. The cigar stand abstains.

lead.headline: Week's count: 1,962 night calls on the tone, and 4,870 on its absence
lead.deck: Night calls fall by 428 on the week, the first fall since July; Monday's calls reckoned apart; Brooklyn Exchange logs 2,210 on the absence; Dr. Rastin's readings since Tuesday 'as before'
lead.body: The Queens Exchange logged 1,962 calls between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. in the seven nights to Friday reporting the tone, against 2,390, the first weekly fall since July, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states. The 4,870 calls of Monday reporting its absence are reckoned apart. The Brooklyn Exchange logged 2,210 calls on the absence and shows 1,166 at its door. Dr. Emil Rastin states that his readings since Tuesday are 'as before.' Queens Light & Power has not yet replied to the Board of Aldermen.

columns.headline: No parcel for Position 43 on a twenty-first Friday
columns.body: No parcel addressed to 'Party Line, Queens Exchange, Position 43' was received yesterday, the twenty-first Friday without one, the supervisor states. The animal attended the parcel window from 4 p.m. to 5 p.m. The warrant for Mr. Joseph Marchetti, lineman, remains outstanding.

columns.headline: Arcade tenants vote to pay the September rent into court on September 3
columns.body: The tenants of the Vantry Arcade voted at the luncheonette last night to deposit the September rent of 412 dollars with the Municipal Court clerk on Tuesday, September 3, Mr. Nathan Ewald states. The clerk will then hold 1,648 dollars. The vote was nine to none, the news and cigar stand abstaining.

columns.headline: Graf Zeppelin 1,900 miles out of Kasumigaura; messages taken at Honolulu
columns.body: The Graf Zeppelin was about 1,900 miles east of Japan at 8 p.m. yesterday, New York time, making 70 miles an hour, the Navy states, by way of its station at Honolulu, which has heard her each hour since noon. Her messages concern fog.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Warm. High 86. Saturday. Calls down. Rent up. Graf out.

lead.headline: Three more licence men caught off the hook, and Crane's count reaches seventeen
lead.deck: The Borough President's clerks go round a second time and find three inspectors who were passed by the colleagues they had just passed; all seventeen still knocking on your door
lead.body: The Borough President's six clerks have gone round Mr. Crane's inspectors a second time and found three more with unlicensed systems at home: three men who were passed earlier this month by colleagues they had just passed themselves. That makes seventeen of sixty-two. All seventeen are still inspecting. Mr. Crane says the law gives them thirty days, like anybody. The Ridgewood landlord has written again, offering to inspect Mr. Crane. Mr. Crane has not said no.

columns.headline: The night calls drop for the first time since July, and the operators hold
columns.body: Nineteen hundred and sixty-two calls about the night tone this week, down four hundred, the first drop since July. Superintendent Arne says Queens is sleeping better since Monday. The operators say Queens is afraid to ring in case it stops again.

columns.headline: The Arcade rings up September, and the clerk's pile heads for sixteen hundred
columns.body: Nine to none at the luncheonette last night, the cigar stand abstaining on account of the pool: September's four hundred and twelve goes in on the third. That makes sixteen hundred and forty-eight dollars held for a company whose whole vocabulary is 'Held.'

columns.headline: The Graf phones in the fog from the middle of the Pacific
columns.body: Honolulu's Navy station hears the Graf every hour now, nineteen hundred miles out of Japan, and every hour she says fog. The Record's window played three fogs last night to a crowd of sixty. The milkman says she should have taken the boat.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Woodside, ten o'clock: Mrs. Fitch's nephew reports the terrier at the Labor Day band rehearsal, in time with the drum. All three owners are on the way. Again.

editorial.headline: The Hum stops and so does the borough
editorial.body: The Hum, which has sounded under Queens at forty-one cycles every night since anyone can remember and which Queens Light & Power swears does not exist, stopped on Monday for a day and a night, and the borough could not sleep for the silence. This paper does not blame Lilith for the Hum. We blame her for everything else. On the silent night a woman's voice was heard in the quiet, singing on the rooftops of Steinway Street, low and sweet, and several readers report that it put them to sleep. The utility says no voice was carried on its lines. The utility, our readers will recall, says the Hum does not exist either.

lead.headline: Astoria Ice Company's mare Nell to retire after twenty seasons
lead.deck: Bay mare of 22 years to leave the Steinway Street route after Labor Day for a farm at Jamaica; a motor truck to take the route; customers asked for their recordings of her bell
lead.body: Nell, a bay mare of 22 years, who has drawn the Astoria Ice Company's wagon on the Steinway Street route for twenty summers, will be retired after Labor Day to a farm at Jamaica, Mr. Gustave Pohl states. The route will be taken by a motor truck. The company estimates that Nell has delivered about 400,000 cakes of ice. Customers on the route have been asked to lend their recordings of her bell for the company's file. Sixty have been received.

columns.headline: Graf Zeppelin about 2,000 miles from the California coast
columns.body: The Graf Zeppelin was about 2,000 miles from the California coast at 8 p.m. yesterday, New York time, the Navy states, her messages being received through Honolulu and concerning fog. The Navy's stations at San Francisco and San Diego have sat since yesterday morning.

columns.headline: Phonautograph Society hears the Long Island City boy's second record
columns.body: The Phonautograph Society's judges have heard a second record by the Long Island City boy whose record of his street at night was set aside, made on Monday at 3 a.m. during the tone's absence, Mr. Linus Fahey, secretary, states. Both records are retained. The Society does not state why.

columns.headline: Stocks close the week at 375.4; tone entered as 'running, high'
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange closed the week at yesterday's short session on a volume of 2,620,000 shares, the industrial average standing at 375.4, the highest in its history and a gain on the week of 13.9. The ticker was 14 minutes late at noon. Its tone was entered as 'running, high.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 83. Sunday. Nell's last week. Bring a carrot.

lead.headline: Nell the ice horse rings her last bell on Steinway Street
lead.deck: Twenty summers, four hundred thousand cakes, one wide straw hat; after Labor Day a motor truck takes the route and does not stop for carrots
lead.body: Twenty summers Nell has pulled the Astoria Ice Company's wagon up Steinway Street, stopping at every door without being told, and after Labor Day a motor truck will do it, faster, and not stop for carrots. Mr. Pohl is sending her to a farm in Jamaica. The company asked the route for its recordings of her bell and has had sixty already, one from a lady who recorded Nell every Thursday for nine years. Nell's hat, the wide one, goes with her.

columns.headline: The quiet night on the record: the Long Island City boy calls back
columns.body: The boy whose minute of his street at three in the morning was set aside by the Society went out again last Monday, the silent night, and recorded the same street. The Society has heard both. It keeps both. It will not say what it heard. The boy says it was his street.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: summer signs off, and Southampton packs its receivers
columns.body: Darlings, the Listening Lady reports Southampton closing up for Labor Day: trunks to the station, recorders crated, and Mrs. Van Ness's mooring-mast hat in a box of its own. The younger Halloran girl is said to be next to marry. The Listening Lady heard it through a door.

columns.headline: The Graf's halfway home, and the Navy on the coast picks up the extension
columns.body: Two thousand miles to California and still fog. Since yesterday the Navy's men at San Francisco and San Diego sit up with Honolulu to hear her come in. Our office boy has moved his blanket from Jackson Avenue to the roof. He says west is that way.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The terrier was not at the band rehearsal. The drum was. All three owners stayed for the concert.

lead.headline: Graf Zeppelin crosses the California coast at the Golden Gate
lead.deck: Ship heard by the Navy's San Francisco station at 8:14 p.m. yesterday, New York time, sixteen minutes before she was seen; about 79 hours from Kasumigaura without a stop; landing at Los Angeles this morning
lead.body: The Graf Zeppelin crossed the coast of California over the Golden Gate at about 8:30 p.m. yesterday, New York time, about 79 hours from Kasumigaura, the Navy states, the first ship of the air to cross the Pacific without a stop. Her engines were heard at the Navy's San Francisco station at 8:14 p.m., sixteen minutes before she was seen. She turned south for Los Angeles, where she is expected at Mines Field this morning. Dr. Hugo Eckener's message read 'Land.'

columns.headline: Mr. Ruth hits his thirty-fourth home run; the Athletics lead by fourteen
columns.body: Mr. Babe Ruth hit his thirty-fourth home run of the season at the Stadium yesterday, the Yankees beating the Detroit Tigers by 6 to 4 before about 40,000. The Athletics won at Philadelphia and lead the American League by fourteen games. Brooklyn and the Giants both lost.

columns.headline: Radio Division hears WORS 1610 at Port Washington for four minutes
columns.body: The Radio Division's men at Port Washington took down figures on 1610 kilocycles for about four minutes from 2:41 a.m. yesterday, Mr. Harold Pike states, the Division's first hearing at any of its places since July. Bay Shore, Long Beach and Montauk heard nothing. Mr. Pike has gone to Port Washington.

columns.headline: Labor Day marshal named; Exchange operators to march with a switchboard
columns.body: The Central Trades and Labor Council of Queens has named Mr. Edward Coyle of the Bricklayers marshal of next Monday's Labor Day parade, the Council states. The Queens Exchange operators will march behind a working switchboard on a motor truck, to be connected to the line at each corner.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Graf Zeppelin was over Santa Barbara at 3:10 a.m., the Navy states, and is circling to await the light.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 82. Monday. The Graf's in Hollywood. Hide the cameras.

lead.headline: Hollywood wants the Graf's picture, and the Graf gives it sound
lead.deck: First ship over the Pacific without a stop comes down at Mines Field; the film men spend a week's wages on nine photographs; everybody else records her for nothing
lead.body: The Graf Zeppelin came down at Mines Field in Los Angeles at four minutes to eight this morning our time, the first airship ever across the Pacific, and the film people were there with their expensive cameras to take her picture, which they did, nine times. The rest of Los Angeles recorded her, as people do. Dr. Eckener's message on crossing the coast last night was one word, 'Land,' which the passengers say was the best word they had heard since Tokyo.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Port Washington picks up four minutes, and Pike drives over
columns.body: Five weeks of nothing, then at nineteen minutes to three yesterday morning the men at Port Washington took down four minutes of figures on sixteen-ten. Mr. Pike drove there before breakfast. Nothing since. The office boy's pin went in at seven. He used the red one.

columns.headline: The Babe connects for thirty-four, but the A's are out of range
columns.body: Number thirty-four for the Babe yesterday against Detroit, a six-to-four win and forty thousand happy. Philadelphia won too and stays fourteen clear. Mr. Huggins says September is long. Our sporting man points out that he said that about August.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Will the switchboard in the parade take calls?'
columns.body: Madam, it will. The Exchange girls march on Labor Day behind a real board on a truck, connected at the corners. You may ring the parade. The operator advises against asking it where your husband is. The parade will be in Jamaica. He may not.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The Cleveland lawyer for the Ditmars house has wired Mr. Crane one word: 'Coming.' Mr. Crane has wired back: 'When.' Cleveland has not.

lead.headline: Mr. Crane's own licence office found to hold an unlicensed system
lead.deck: Office at Borough Hall inspected at 10 a.m. yesterday by Mr. Otto Lentz, the Ridgewood landlord whose question began the inspection of the inspectors; system installed 1922 and never applied for; licensed by 11:20 a.m.
lead.body: Mr. Hollis Crane's licence office at Borough Hall was found yesterday to have an unlicensed listening system, his office states, on inspection by Mr. Otto Lentz, the Ridgewood landlord whose question began the inspection of the office's inspectors, at Mr. Crane's invitation. The system was installed in 1922 and was never applied for. Mr. Crane applied for its licence at 11:15 a.m., to his own office, and granted it at 11:20 a.m. under section 4. Mr. Lentz was thanked.

columns.headline: Graf Zeppelin lands at Los Angeles; to leave for Lakehurst tonight
columns.body: The Graf Zeppelin landed at Mines Field, Los Angeles, at 7:56 a.m. yesterday, New York time, the Navy states. About 150,000 persons were present. She will leave for Lakehurst tonight by way of Chicago, on the last stage of her flight round the world.

columns.headline: Stocks rise to 378.2 on 4,910,000 shares; ticker 26 minutes late
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange rose yesterday on a volume of 4,910,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 378.2, a gain of 2.8 and the highest in its history. The ticker ran 26 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'running, high.'

columns.headline: Light company's written reply to the Board of Aldermen due by Friday
columns.body: Queens Light & Power states that its written reply to the Board of Aldermen on the events of August 19 will be delivered by Friday, the tenth day. Alderman John Feeney states that he will read it to the Board 'as received.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night at Port Washington, where Mr. Pike sat, the Radio Division states.

columns.headline: Public schools of Queens to open September 9; registration next week
columns.body: The public schools of Queens will open on September 9, the Board of Education states. New pupils may be registered at the school nearest their home from next Tuesday. Evening classes in English and bookkeeping will begin on September 23.

columns.headline: Long Island potato growers expect a heavy crop; prices ease
columns.body: Growers in Suffolk County expect a heavy potato crop, the growers' association states, with digging to begin next week. Prices eased at the Wallabout Market yesterday. Duck shipments from Eastport were moderate. Sound apples remained scarce.

columns.headline: Furnished rooms, Woodside: two gentlemen preferred, near the Flushing line
columns.body: Two furnished rooms, front, in a private house at Woodside, five minutes from the Flushing line. Clean, quiet, with use of bath. Gentlemen preferred, and board by arrangement. Apply to the owner on the premises, any evening after six.

columns.headline: Mrs. Louise Thaden first at Cleveland in the women's air derby
columns.body: Mrs. Louise Thaden landed first at Cleveland yesterday in the women's air derby from Santa Monica, flying a Travel Air in the heavier class, the wire states. The derby was nine days on the way. One flier was killed in Arizona and several were forced down; most reached Cleveland.

back.foot: The Borough Record, Long Island City. Corrections are printed as received.

speaker.ear: Warm. High 85. Tuesday. The landlord inspected the inspector. Guess.

lead.headline: The landlord inspects Crane, and Borough Hall is caught off the record
lead.deck: Mr. Lentz of Ridgewood, who started it all by asking an inspector for his licence, is invited in to look at the licence office itself; a system from 1922, never applied for; five minutes to fix it
lead.body: It had to happen. Mr. Lentz, the Ridgewood landlord who asked an inspector for his licence and started the whole business, was invited yesterday to inspect Mr. Crane's own office at Borough Hall. He found a system put in in 1922 that nobody had ever licensed. Mr. Crane applied for a licence at a quarter past eleven, to himself, and granted it at twenty past, the fastest licence in Queens. Mr. Lentz was thanked. He says he would do it again.

columns.headline: The Graf ties up in Los Angeles, and a hundred and fifty thousand tune in
columns.body: Mines Field yesterday: a hundred and fifty thousand people, two hundred film men and one airship that had come from Tokyo without stopping. The film men took nine pictures and spent a week's wages. Everybody else recorded her for nothing. Tonight she leaves for home, by Chicago.

columns.headline: The light company promises its letter by Friday, and Feeney tunes up
columns.body: The company says its letter to the Aldermen about the nineteenth will arrive by Friday, the tenth day, as asked. Alderman Feeney says he will read it to the Board aloud. He is practising in his office on the Exchange's call log, which takes him four hours.

columns.headline: Wall Street plays it high again, and the ticker runs behind the band
columns.body: Three hundred and seventy-eight on the industrials, another record, and the ticker twenty-six minutes behind. The tone book says 'running, high.' A Flushing undertaker tells us he has bought more Radio. We asked why. He says he likes the sound of it.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Los Angeles, eleven tonight our time: the Graf is away east. Lakehurst says Thursday. Queens says it will listen.

lead.headline: About 9,000 to march in Queens Labor Day parade; Exchange operators to join
lead.deck: Sixty-one unions from Jamaica Avenue at 168th Street to King Park, starting at 10 a.m. Monday; operators behind a working switchboard on a motor truck; the Ice Drivers to march with the mare Nell
lead.body: About 9,000 members of 61 unions will march in the Labor Day parade of the Central Trades and Labor Council of Queens on Monday, from Jamaica Avenue at 168th Street to King Park, starting at 10 a.m., Mr. Edward Coyle, marshal, states. The Queens Exchange operators will march for the first time, behind a working switchboard on a motor truck. The Ice Drivers' Union will march with Nell, the Astoria Ice Company's mare, on her last day in harness. The Interborough will run 40 extra trains.

columns.headline: Mr. Gorman asks for the calendar of September 23; 'twenty-seven days'
columns.body: Mr. Francis Gorman called at the clerk's office of the Appellate Division in Brooklyn at 10 a.m. yesterday and asked for the calendar for September 23, the clerk states. None has been printed. Mr. Gorman stated that it was 'twenty-seven days' and left. Four other persons were in the office.

columns.headline: Senate vault's record of March 27 unclaimed in its twenty-third week
columns.body: Mr. Lyman Pratt, Clerk of the Senate, states that the committee room's record of March 27 containing the word 'resent' remains unclaimed in the vault at Albany in its twenty-third week. Senator Rufus Keel has not written this week. Mr. Pratt has written to the Senator to ask whether he is well.

columns.headline: Graf Zeppelin over El Paso and Kansas City; due over Chicago today
columns.body: The Graf Zeppelin was over El Paso, Texas, at noon yesterday, New York time, and over Kansas City at 11 p.m., the Navy states. She is expected over Chicago this afternoon and over this city at about dawn tomorrow, on her way to Lakehurst.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 84. Wednesday. Tomorrow, early. Set your alarm. Or don't.

lead.headline: Get up on the roof at dawn: the Graf comes home on the long-distance line
lead.deck: Kansas City behind her, Chicago this afternoon, and tomorrow at first light she crosses the city for Lakehurst; you will hear her before you see her, so listen north-west
lead.body: The Graf Zeppelin is over the middle of America tonight, Kansas City behind her and Chicago this afternoon, and tomorrow at about dawn she comes over the city on her way to Lakehurst, the last few miles of the first trip round the world by air. You will hear her before you see her; Montauk heard her three hundred miles off this month, so Queens should get a good long earful. Go up on the roof. Take a blanket. Take the office boy. He knows the way.

columns.headline: Gorman says twenty-seven, and Brooklyn starts counting along on the line
columns.body: Tuesday, ten o'clock, the clerk's window: the calendar for the twenty-third of September, please. Not printed. 'Twenty-seven days.' Out. Mr. Gorman now has company: three law clerks and a newsboy stood behind him yesterday, counting with him under their breath.

columns.headline: Week twenty-three: Keel goes quiet, and the clerk rings to ask after him
columns.body: Twenty-three weeks for 'resent' in the vault at Albany, and this week no letter from Senator Keel. Mr. Pratt has written to him to ask whether he is well. That makes the clerk the one asking now. The Speaker is asking too.

columns.headline: Nell rings in Labor Day at the head of the line
columns.body: Nell, Mr. Pohl's ice mare, marches on Labor Day with the Ice Drivers, her last day in harness. Nine thousand will follow her down Jamaica Avenue, among them the Exchange girls with a switchboard on a truck. Bring carrots for Nell. Bring a nickel for the switchboard.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Chicago, two this afternoon: the Graf over the Loop, and the Loop stopped work to hear her. Next stop, us.

record.ear: Fair, cool at dawn. High 80. Low 63.

lead.headline: Graf Zeppelin passes over Chicago and Cleveland; due over this city at dawn
lead.deck: Over the Loop at 2:05 p.m., over Cleveland at 9:40 p.m.; the Navy's stations from Selfridge Field to Lakehurst sit through the night; ground crew of 350 report at 3 a.m.
lead.body: The Graf Zeppelin passed over Chicago at 2:05 p.m. yesterday, New York time, and over Cleveland at 9:40 p.m., the Navy states, on the last stage of her flight round the world. She is expected over this city at about dawn today and at Lakehurst by 8 a.m. The Navy's stations from Selfridge Field to Lakehurst sat through the night. The ground crew of 350 reported at 3 a.m. This newspaper's window on Jackson Avenue opened at 4 a.m.

columns.headline: Cleveland attorney for the Ditmars Avenue estate to attend on September 10
columns.body: Mr. Royal Haskin, the Cleveland attorney who answered the Queens Signal Exchange's advertisement for the owner of the house on Ditmars Avenue, will attend at Mr. Hollis Crane's office on September 10 with his client's papers, the office states. The seal remains until then.

columns.headline: Stocks ease to 377.6 on 4,300,000 shares; tone entered as 'high, held'
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange eased yesterday on a volume of 4,300,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 377.6, a loss of 0.6. The ticker ran 17 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'high, held.'

columns.headline: Hague conference near agreement on reparations; hall's record 212 hours
columns.body: The conference of the powers at The Hague on German reparations is near agreement, the State Department states, the British delegation having accepted a revised division of payments. The Dutch Government states that the hall's recorders now hold 212 hours of the conference, 'for the delegations' use only.'

record.wire: LATE WIRE: The Navy states that the Graf Zeppelin's engines were heard over Paterson, N.J., at 4:52 a.m.

speaker.ear: Cool. High 80. Thursday. She's home. Queens heard her first.

lead.headline: Queens hears the Graf before it sees her, and the whole borough picks up
lead.deck: Eight minutes past five, a second hum on top of the first, from the north-west; eleven minutes of sound and nothing to see; then silver over the Palisades and every roof in the borough cheering
lead.body: At eight minutes past five this morning a second hum came down on Queens, on top of the first, low and steady, from the north-west, and all over the borough people climbed onto roofs in nightclothes to look at nothing. For eleven minutes there was only sound. Then, over the Palisades, silver against a pink sky, there she was, round the world in three weeks, turning down over Manhattan for Lakehurst. Corona cheered. Woodside cheered. The operators took nine hundred calls asking whether it was her. It was her.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Was that her, or was that the Hum?'
columns.body: Madam, both. The tone was there all along, as usual; the Graf's engines came in over it, higher, and the operator, who has heard the tone every night for a year, says she could tell the two apart at once. She says the Graf's was the one that was leaving.

columns.headline: Lakehurst ties her up, and the world's longest call ends at the mast
columns.body: She came down at Lakehurst at thirteen minutes past eight, twenty-one days and some hours from Lakehurst to Lakehurst, the first ship round the world by air. Dr. Eckener told the mast recorder it had been 'long, but quiet.' Lady Drummond-Hay told it she wanted a bath.

columns.headline: The dog war: the terrier goes up on the roof to hear the ship come in on cue
columns.body: Ruthie Danko took the terrier up on her Sunnyside roof this morning to hear the Graf, and at eight minutes past five he barked once, at about A, the judges' note. Mrs. Fitch says she heard it from Woodside and would know that bark anywhere. So, she says, would the Graf.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Queens Light & Power, asked whether the morning's second hum was the Graf, states that it does not comment on airships.

lead.headline: Graf Zeppelin completes her flight round the world at Lakehurst
lead.deck: Engines heard in Queens from 5:08 a.m., eleven minutes before the ship was sighted over the Palisades; made fast at the mast at 8:13 a.m.; Queens Exchange logs 912 calls asking whether it was she
lead.body: The Graf Zeppelin was made fast to the mast at the Naval Air Station at Lakehurst at 8:13 a.m. yesterday, completing the first flight round the world by air in about 21 days from Lakehurst to Lakehurst, the Navy states. Her engines were heard in Queens from 5:08 a.m., eleven minutes before she was sighted over the Palisades. The Queens Exchange logged 912 calls between 5 a.m. and 6 a.m. asking whether it was she. Dr. Hugo Eckener stated to the mast recorder that the flight had been 'long, but quiet.'

columns.headline: Light company delivers its one-page reply to the Board of Aldermen
columns.body: Queens Light & Power delivered its written reply to the Board of Aldermen at 4:50 p.m. yesterday, a day before it was due, Alderman John Feeney states. The reply is of one page. It states that the company's system 'operated normally throughout August 19.' Mr. Feeney will read it to the Board on Tuesday.

columns.headline: Stocks rise to 380.1 on 4,150,000 shares; tone entered as 'high'
columns.body: Prices on the Stock Exchange rose yesterday on a volume of 4,150,000 shares, the industrial average closing at 380.1, a gain of 2.5 and the highest in its history. The ticker ran 18 minutes late at the close. The tone book records its tone at 3 p.m. as 'high.'

columns.headline: Board of Estimate rescinds the Borden Avenue gates 11 to 5
columns.body: The Board of Estimate yesterday rescinded by 11 votes to 5 the gates at the Borden Avenue crossing, passed 16 to 0 on March 28, no work having begun. It acted on the report of its acting engineer for Queens that the item is 'not urgent.' The petitioners were not heard. The work may be applied for in 1931.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 81. Friday. Twenty-two Fridays. Last Derby before the final.

lead.headline: Pun Derby, week thirteen: the Graf's homecoming cards land the prize
lead.deck: A Corona operator writes the winner on the back of a milk ticket at five in the morning on her roof; the grand final set for Labor Day at the King Park bandstand; the horse is ruled out of order again
lead.body: Week thirteen, the airship special, goes to Miss Dolores Ianelli, telephone operator, of Corona, who was on her roof at five yesterday morning and wrote it on the back of a milk ticket: 'The Graf went round the world in twenty-one days. My brother can't get round the block without stopping to talk.' Five dollars and a year's Speaker. Runner-up: 'The Zeppelin is like a party line. You hear it coming, and you can't get off.' Mr. Kehoe's horse sent a card about a hay balloon. Disqualified. Final Monday.

columns.headline: Party Line's twenty-second Friday, and the parcel window won't put her through
columns.body: Twenty-two Fridays. Party Line at the window at four. At ten past, the supervisor, worn thin by the Graf's nine hundred calls, brought her a saucer. At five, under the board. No tin from Corona. Sergeant Moran bowled a strike on Wednesday and was congratulated, as Smith.

columns.headline: The light company writes one page: the line was fine on the nineteenth
columns.body: A day early, one page, delivered to Alderman Feeney at ten to five yesterday: the company's system 'operated normally throughout August 19.' That is the whole letter. Mr. Feeney will read it to the Board on Tuesday. He says it will not take four hours.

columns.headline: The inspection reaches the clerks, and the Borough President is on hold
columns.body: The six borrowed clerks have finished inspecting Mr. Crane's sixty-two inspectors: seventeen unlicensed in all. Now the Borough President has asked that his clerks' houses be inspected, by Mr. Crane's men. Mr. Lentz of Ridgewood has asked to come. Nobody has asked the Borough President.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Lakehurst, six o'clock: the Graf's passengers scattered for trains. Dr. Eckener stayed at the mast an hour, listening to his engines cool.

record.ear: Fair. High 82. Low 65. Fair for Labor Day, the Bureau states.

lead.headline: Industrial average closes August at 380.3, the highest in its history
lead.deck: Rise of about 22 points in the month on about 95,000,000 shares; brokers' loans at a record; tone book enters 'high' or 'running, high' on 15 of 26 trading days; Queens brokers' wires open to 9 p.m.
lead.body: The industrial average of stocks closed August at 380.3 yesterday, a rise of about 22 points in the month and the highest in its history, the Exchange's figures show. About 95,000,000 shares changed hands in the month. Brokers' loans stand at a record. The tone book entered the ticker's tone at 3 p.m. as 'high' or 'running, high' on 15 of 26 trading days, and as 'dropped, hollow' on one. Brokers in Jamaica and Flushing have kept their wires open until 9 p.m. since Tuesday.

columns.headline: Week's count: 2,104 night calls on the tone; Brooklyn door at 1,214
columns.body: The Queens Exchange logged 2,104 calls between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. in the seven nights to Friday reporting the tone, against 1,962, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states. The 912 calls of Thursday morning concerning the Graf Zeppelin are reckoned apart. The Brooklyn Exchange's door shows 1,214.

columns.headline: No parcel for Position 43 on a twenty-second Friday
columns.body: No parcel addressed to 'Party Line, Queens Exchange, Position 43' was received yesterday, the twenty-second Friday without one, the supervisor states. The animal attended the parcel window from 4 p.m. to 5 p.m. The warrant for Mr. Joseph Marchetti, lineman, remains outstanding.

columns.headline: Hague conference agrees on the Young plan; each delegation given its record
columns.body: The conference of the powers at The Hague reached agreement on the Young plan for German reparations early today, their time, the State Department states. Mr. Philip Snowden has secured a larger share of the payments for Great Britain. The Dutch Government has given each delegation its own record of the hall.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states, at any of its four places.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 82. Saturday. Labor Day Monday. Everybody off the line.

lead.headline: Summer rings off for Labor Day, and Queens falls in on the line
lead.deck: The Graf went round, the Babe got to five hundred, the market went up like a balloon and the Hum took a day off; Monday nine thousand march, and Tuesday the Arcade pays September into court
lead.body: It was the summer the Graf went round the world, the Babe got to five hundred, the market went up like a balloon and the Hum went away for a day and came back. On Monday nine thousand Queens workers march down Jamaica Avenue, the Exchange girls with their switchboard on a truck and Nell the ice horse at the front, on her last day. On Tuesday the Arcade pays September into court. The light company says August 19 was normal. The Speaker says it was the day we all heard ourselves think, and didn't care for it.

columns.headline: Twenty-one hundred calls, and the Hum settles back into the night shift
columns.body: Two thousand one hundred and four calls about the night tone this week, up a little. The operators' sheets say 'steady.' Dr. Rastin says two fifths over June, as before. The light company has said its one page. The Hum has said nothing new, which, after the nineteenth, Queens will take.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Will the company ring for its money?'
columns.body: Sir, the company has no telephone. On Tuesday Mr. Ewald carries September to the court clerk, who will then hold sixteen hundred and forty-eight dollars for Signal Ground Rents Inc. The company's last word was 'Held.' The operator has been saying it all summer, and nobody has paid her.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Port Washington's four minutes stand alone on the map
columns.body: Six nights since Port Washington's four minutes, and nothing at any of Mr. Pike's places. The office boy's red pin stands alone on the north shore. He says it is waiting for a friend. The editor has ordered more pins, in case.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Kehoe's horse has been entered in Monday's Pun Derby final under the name Kehoe. The judges are considering it.

editorial.headline: The airship is heard before it is seen
editorial.body: The Graf Zeppelin came home over the city on Thursday, heard on every rooftop half an hour before it was seen, and half the borough stood on the roofs to watch it. The other half watched a lady in black standing on the tallest of the Queensboro Bridge's towers, quite still, with her cape spread to the wind like the airship's own shadow, until the Zeppelin passed over her, when she bowed. Nobody knows how she got up there. Nobody knows how she got down. This paper knows only that women, as every editor knows, are heard before they are seen. With this one it is the other way round. We find it unnerving.
